PARALLEL RESONANT CIRCUITS
OBJECTIVES
w Calculate and measure the resonant frequency in a LCR parallel circuit.
w Observe the values of It and Zt below resonance, at resonance, and above resonance in a parallel LCR circuit...
. The experiment in this lesson is not setup to use the selected trainer.
EQUIPMENT REQUIRED
Nida Experiment Card PC130 - 20A
In this lesson you will verify normal operation of LCR parallel resonant circuits by calculating and measuring the resonant frequency.

LESSON MENU
The purpose of this experiment is to demonstrate the normal operation of LCR parallel resonant circuits.
EXPERIMENT
Pick up the PC130-20A card. This card is used to demonstrate the operation of LCR parallel resonant circuits.
Compare the card with the schematic shown.
Notice that there are four LCR parallel circuits. S1, S2, S3, and S4 are used to select the circuit.
On the PC card, when a switch is to the left the circuit is open. When a switch is to the right, power is applied.
In this experiment you will use circuit A only. Circuits B, C, and D operate the same, only the values are different.
Notice that the circuit is a tank circuit. There is no parallel resistance.
Resistor R1 is a small value resistor (sampling resistor) that is used to measure total circuit current.
Remember, measuring the voltage drop across R1 and dividing by the value of R1 equals total current since R1 is in series to L1 and C1, (I = E/R).

The LCR circuit is operating normally at resonance.
Now, let's look at the characteristics of a parallel resonant circuit.
The best way to observe these characteristics is to construct a graph. The graph shows the effect of frequency on circuit values.
Let's measure and graph total circuit current. Remember,
1. Ensure that S1 is to the right on PC130-20A.
2. Ensure that the output of the function generator is 5 Vpp as measured at TP10 on PC130-20A.
MEASUREMENT SETUP - Connect CH1 probe to TP10.
3. Connect CH1 probe to TP3 on PC130-20A. This measures the voltage drop across sampling resistor, R1.
MEASUREMENT SETUP - Connect CH1 probe to TP3.
4. Adjust the function generators frequency until Er1 is minimum. You should measure approximately .015 Vpp..
Do not adjust the function generator below 10 kHz or above 100 kHz... kHz. - 5
Do not adjust the function generator below 10 kHz or above 100 kHz. - 5
With .015 Vpp across R1 and a resistance of 100 ohms, total current equals .15 mA. A dot is placed at the intersection of .15 mA and 30 kHz.
5. Raise the frequency of the function generator to 40 kHz.
Notice that R1's voltage drop increased to approximately
6. Lower the frequency of the function generator to 20 kHz. Notice that Er1 is approximately .25 Vpp or It of 2.5 mA (.25/100).
7. Raise the frequency of the function generator to 50 kHz. Notice that Er1 is approximately .3 Vpp or an It of 3mA..
8. Lower the frequency of the function generator to 10 kHz. Notice that Er1 is approximately .8 Vpp or It of 8mA.
9. Raise the frequency of the function generator to 60 kHz. Notice that Er1 is approximately .45 Vpp or It of 4.5 mA.
Connecting the dots vividly illustrates that total current is minimum at resonance in a parallel circuit.
Total circuit impedance can also be illustrated by a graph. Remember, the applied voltage divided by total current equals total impedance.
